opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most interesting asymmetries in the field right now. With language, we got incredibly lucky. Humanity spent decades putting an enormous amount of text onto the internet, and it happened to be this rich, compressed record of human knowledge and reasoning. So when we showed up with transformers and enough compute, the data was just sitting there waiting for us.

Biology and robotics don't have that. In robotics especially, there's no internet-scale corpus of robots interacting with the physical world. Every trajectory you collect costs real time, real hardware, real people supervising it. You can't just scrape it. And the data is also very embodiment-specific: what one arm with one gripper learned doesn't trivially transfer to a different platform.

Biology is a bit different. There's actually a lot of data in some sense, sequences, structures, assays, but it's fragmented, noisy, and often locked inside individual labs or companies. And critically, much of it lacks the closed-loop signal you want. You have observations, but not always the interventions and outcomes that let a model learn causal structure.

So I think the path forward in both looks similar. First, simulation and synthetic data, generating environments where models can explore cheaply, and then working hard on closing the sim-to-real gap. Second, leaning on the general models we already have. Language models carry a surprising amount of world knowledge and can bootstrap reasoning in these domains. Third, building the data flywheel deliberately: getting systems deployed, even imperfectly, so they collect the data that makes them better.

But I'd be honest that it's a slower grind. Language felt like a sudden unlock because the data existed. In these domains, we have to build the data along with the models, and that takes time and capital. I'm optimistic, but I don't think it'll look like the overnight leap we saw with text.

r001.rationale: The response describes biology data as plentiful but fragmented and locked in labs or companies. For robotics, it instead emphasizes the lack of an internet-scale corpus and the cost of collecting data, not restricted access to siloed data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to understand it is that language got lucky. We had this massive, free, pre-existing corpus sitting on the internet that humans had spent decades generating for their own reasons, and it just happened to be the perfect training signal. Biology and robotics didn't get that gift.

In biology, the data that exists is sparse and expensive and often not the data you actually want. You've got sequence data, sure, and that's where you've seen progress, like protein structure prediction. But the really valuable stuff, which is how a perturbation plays out in a living system, what a drug does in a human body, that's locked behind wet lab experiments that cost real money and real time. You can't scrape your way to a cure. And the data that does exist tends to be fragmented across institutions, collected under different protocols, with very little standardization. So you don't have one big clean corpus, you have ten thousand little inconsistent ones.

Robotics is the same story from a different direction. The internet has essentially zero data about what it feels like to pick up a cup. There's no torque readings, no tactile feedback, no proprioception sitting on Reddit. So you have to generate it yourself, and generating it means either running real robots, which is slow and breaks hardware, or running simulation, which is fast but has this persistent gap to reality that people have been fighting for a decade.

So the honest framing is that in those domains, the bottleneck isn't the model architecture anymore. The transformer's fine. The bottleneck is that you have to go out and build the data generation engine first, and that looks a lot more like running a lab or a factory than it does like training a model. The groups that win there are going to be the ones that figure out how to turn data collection into a flywheel, where the model gets good enough to make the next round of experiments cheaper or more targeted, and you compound from there. That's a very different shape of company than the ones that won on language.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fragmented, inconsistent biological datasets and data locked behind experiments, but frames the broader problem as sparse data and a lack of a large corpus. It does not clearly identify restricted access to siloed data rather than insufficient total data.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge in both is that the data you need isn’t necessarily sitting on the internet waiting to be collected. With language, we had this enormous body of text that people had already produced. In biology and robotics, you often have to go out and generate the observations that would let you learn the thing you care about.

In biology, you might have lots of observational data, but answering a particular question requires running an experiment. That can be expensive and slow. In robotics, a video can show you what an action looks like, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you the forces involved, what the robot sensed, or what would have happened if it had taken a different action.

So I see the problem as partly about building a good data-generation loop: use the model to decide what experiment or interaction would be informative, collect that data, and learn from it. Simulation can help, particularly in robotics, but you still have to establish that what you learn transfers to the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes needing to generate task-relevant observations and experiments, but does not identify restricted access to siloed data as the problem or distinguish it from insufficient total data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge in both domains is that the data you want isn’t necessarily data that already exists in a useful form. With text, we had this enormous body of material that humans had already produced and put online. In biology and robotics, a lot of the information you need has to be generated through experiments or interactions with the physical world, and that can be slow and expensive.

There’s also a distinction between having lots of data and having the right data. In biology, you might have a huge number of measurements, but you want to understand what happens when you intervene. In robotics, watching a video of someone doing something doesn’t give you the same information as taking an action and observing the result.

So I’d frame it as a problem of building a learning loop: use the data you have, identify what you’re uncertain about, and collect the next experiment or interaction that will teach you the most. Simulation and synthetic data can help, but ultimately you need some way to check those predictions against the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes data that must be generated through costly experiments or physical interactions, and a need for the right data. It does not identify restricted access to siloed data as the problem.
